claims.text: Dynamic mechanical behavior in solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn is controlled by elastic strain-induced amorphization.
Elastic strain-induced amorphization limits conventional dislocation nucleation.
The proposed amorphization mechanism sustains a strength-ductility balance.
The tested FeNiCrMn material is single-phase, chemically homogeneous, and has minimal pre-existing defects.
High elastic strain produces local amorphous regions through a loss of lattice ordering.
Local atomic-environment or chemical inhomogeneity depresses conventional dislocation nucleation in HEAs.
The Co-free FeNiCrMn system possesses local chemical inhomogeneities that depress dislocation nucleation.
The FeNiCrMn lattice locally becomes amorphous when applied elastic strain approaches approximately 10%.
Strain-induced amorphization softens dislocation activity and modulates strain hardening.
The onset of amorphization varies with temperature and strain rate.
Changes in amorphization onset govern the balance between strength and ductility.
Lower temperatures or higher strain rates may shift the threshold strain for amorphization.
A shift in the amorphization threshold will produce observable changes in yield stress and strain-hardening rate.
Localized loss of lattice order will coincide with a decline in dislocation density.
At extreme temperatures or strain rates, twinning or phase transformations may become significant.
In tensile tests of a series of HEAs, sudden loss of lattice ordering was observed at approximately 10% elastic strain.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as having a homogeneous chemical distribution, whereas the mechanism invokes inherent local chemical inhomogeneities. These could coexist if macroscopic and atomic-scale homogeneity were distinguished, but that scale distinction is not stated.
